definition: A vital substance the body needs for growth, energy production and maintenance of bodily functions.
Protein, carbohydrate or fat: supplies energy (calories) for daily functioning and repair.
A vitamin or mineral: essential, needed in small amounts, supports functions rather than supplying energy.
A source with all essential amino acids: eggs, milk, soybean.
Severe protein deficiency in children: edema and growth failure.
Whey is fast-absorbing (pre/post-workout); casein is slow-digesting (before bed).
How fast a food raises blood sugar; high-GI spikes and crashes, low-GI releases slowly.
Fruit sugar that the liver metabolises into fat, unlike glucose, which is burned or stored as glycogen.
Acetate, propionate and butyrate, made when gut bacteria ferment fibre; the colonocytes' main fuel.
A soluble, gel-forming fibre supplement for constipation, cholesterol and blood sugar.
Processed, hydrogenated fat that raises heart-disease risk; avoid completely.
Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease: excess fat in the liver, linked to obesity and insulin resistance.
A, D, E and K: stored in fatty tissue and liver, so excess can cause toxicity.
B-group and C: not stored, excess excreted in urine; must be eaten regularly.
Toxicity from excess vitamins, mainly fat-soluble A (liver damage) and D (hypercalcaemia).
High blood calcium from excess vitamin D: nausea, weakness, kidney damage.
Vitamin D deficiency bone disease: rickets in children, osteomalacia in adults.
Vitamin C deficiency: bleeding gums, joint pain, weakness, anaemia.
Vitamin B1 (thiamine) deficiency.
Vitamin B3 (niacin) deficiency, the '3 Ds'.
Anaemia and fatigue from vitamin B12 deficiency; vegans are at risk.
Birth defects linked to folic acid (B9) deficiency in pregnancy.
Enlarged thyroid from iodine deficiency.
Iron overload that harms organs.
The energy needed to raise 1 kg of water by 1 °C.
A product that adds nutrients to the diet, complementing food intake.
A food that provides health benefits beyond basic nutrition (probiotic yoghurt, green tea, oats).
A nutrient-rich food; largely a marketing term.
A bioactive compound with health benefits that requires clinical evidence; sits between food and drug.
The fraction of an ingested dose that is absorbed and reaches the body; plain curcumin extract is about 1%.
Formulations that protect a compound and boost absorption (Meriva curcumin about 50×, liposomal glutathione).
Fast, non-specific, immediate defence with no memory (macrophages, neutrophils).
Slow, targeted defence that builds memory against specific pathogens (T-cells, B-cells).
The most abundant white blood cell; rapid defence against infection.
Immune cell that produces antibodies.
The chemical language of immunity: pro-inflammatory (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α), anti-inflammatory (IL-10, IL-4), interferons, chemokines.
Cytokines that provide antiviral defence.
Short-term, protective, self-limiting response: redness, heat, swelling, fever.
Persistent low-grade immune activation linked to diabetes, CVD, autoimmunity, depression.
Advanced glycation end products: sugar stuck to proteins, driving inflammation and oxidative stress.
The immune system attacking the body's own tissue, e.g. type 1 diabetes.
Excessive inflammatory response, the driver of severe COVID-19.
Thai herb officially recommended for mild COVID-19; Thailand's best-selling domestic herbal supplement.
An imbalance in gut microbiota: fewer good microbes, more harmful ones, less diversity.
Disruption of tight junctions in the gut barrier, linked to inflammation and metabolic dysfunction.
The absorptive cell lining the small intestine.
Live microorganisms that confer a health benefit in adequate amounts; strain-identified, proven in humans.
A fermentable fibre that selectively stimulates beneficial gut bacteria (inulin, FOS, GOS, resistant starch).
Non-living microbial metabolites or components that confer benefits (SCFAs, heat-killed cells); stable at room temperature.
A combination of a probiotic and a prebiotic.
Colony forming units, the dose unit for probiotics (typically 1–100 billion a day).
A gut bacterium low in obesity and diabetes; restoring it improves glucose and fat regulation.
Incretin hormone that boosts insulin, slows gastric emptying and increases satiety; GLP-1 RA drugs include semaglutide.
Three or more of: abdominal obesity, high triglycerides, low HDL, high blood pressure, high fasting glucose.
Total years lived.
Years lived without chronic disease.
Pushing illness into the fewest final years of life.
Shortening of chromosome ends with each cell division; a hallmark of ageing.
'Zombie' cells that stop dividing and secrete SASP, ageing their neighbours.
Chronic low-grade inflammation of ageing, driven by SASP.
Age-related decline of the immune system.
DNA methylation-based measure; the most accurate biological-age predictor (Horvath, GrimAge).
Oxygen molecules that damage DNA, proteins and lipids in excess but act as essential signals at low levels.
Beneficial adaptation to a small stress, such as low-level ROS during exercise.
The master cellular antioxidant; poor oral bioavailability; may feed tumours.
NAD+ precursors; oral NAD+ itself is only 2–10% bioavailable.
A compound that clears senescent cells, e.g. quercetin with fisetin.
Regions of exceptional longevity: plant-dominant diet, natural movement, purpose and social ties.
Two-way communication between gut and brain via the vagus nerve; 90–95% of serotonin is made in the gut.
Cumulative wear on body and brain from chronic stress.
A herb that enhances stress resilience, e.g. ashwagandha, ginseng, rhodiola.
